sections.body: The internet is a giant network of computers connected by cables, Wi-Fi, phone signals and even undersea cables.
When you send a message, it's split into small PACKETS. They travel separately and are put back together at the other end.
Each device has an address (an IP address) so packets know where to go, a bit like a postal address.
Most internet data between continents travels through cables under the ocean, not through satellites.

quiz.q: What happens to a message sent over the internet?
options: It's split into packets and put back together
It travels as one huge piece
hints: Big things are easier to send in pieces.
Moving house, you pack things into boxes and unpack them at the new home. Internet data works similarly.
quiz.explain: Messages are split into packets, sent, then reassembled.

quiz.q: How does internet data mostly travel between continents?
hints: The lesson's fact box mentions this.
Satellites are used sometimes, but most data uses something laid on the sea floor.
quiz.explain: Most data between continents travels through undersea cables.

quiz.q: What is an IP address used for?
options: It tells packets which device to go to
It is the password for your Wi-Fi
It measures how fast the internet is
hints: Every device on the internet has one.
The lesson compares it to a postal address.
Example: a letter has a house address on it. That tells the post office where to deliver it.
quiz.explain: An IP address is like a postal address. It tells packets which device to go to.
